chapters.title: Compare four ways to support the work
chapters.transcript:
Before we choose technology, we need to be clear about the work. Open the workflow you mapped in Lesson Two point One. Keep your reviewed communication from Lesson Two point Three beside it. What small part of that process needs help? What information enters? What result should leave? Who checks that result? These questions give us something useful to compare.

We will consider four support patterns. A support pattern is simply a way to arrange the work and the help around it. The first is no AI. A person uses a checklist, an approved template, or an existing ordinary tool. This can be a good choice when the work is occasional, the details are sensitive, or a conversation needs careful human judgment. No AI does not mean no organization or no technology.

The second is an assistant. You give it a directed request and inspect its response. It might draft a reminder from approved facts, summarize a record, or identify missing details. For this lesson, that help ends with a draft or a recommendation. A person checks and approves any real use. Some products called assistants can also use tools. The name alone does not tell us what permissions they have.

The third is rule-based automation. A trigger starts the work. A trigger might be a scheduled date or a confirmed change in a record. Defined rules then control what happens. If an invoice is overdue and the required checks pass, prepare an approved reminder. If the record shows a dispute, stop that routine path. Ordinary automation does not have to use AI.

The fourth is an agent. Within its permitted scope, it may choose several steps or tools to pursue a goal. That flexibility can help when the next step cannot always be set in advance. It also means we need clear limits, monitoring, and a way to stop. An agent is not automatically the best choice because it can do more.

Imagine a community group updating a small volunteer list once a month. A clear checklist may be sufficient. Imagine a service team drafting varied explanations from approved notes. An assistant may help. Imagine a repeated, fixed reminder with reliable records. Automation may fit. Compare the work, the oversight effort, and the consequences. Your task is to choose the least complex suitable pattern, not to make every process more autonomous.

chapters.title: Keep the invoice exception with a person
chapters.transcript:
Let us compare the same task under all four patterns. This is a fictional training case. A small service company wants help with invoice reminders. Its fictional procedure permits a standard reminder only when the invoice is seven days overdue, the balance is confirmed unpaid, the recipient is verified, and no dispute or payment arrangement is recorded. Those are the rules of this example, not general business requirements.

With no AI, the accounts coordinator checks the record, uses the approved template, and keeps a note of the review. This is a reasonable baseline. If the team handles only a few reminders, the checklist might solve the problem without adding another system. Do not invent a time saving. Keep any expected improvement separate from a result you have actually observed.

With an assistant, the coordinator supplies authorized facts and asks for a draft. The assistant might help make the next action clearer. It may also make an error. The coordinator checks the amount, recipient, status, and wording before approving use. In our bounded concept, the assistant has no permission to send messages, alter records, or approve an adjustment.

With rule-based automation, a defined trigger can start a series of fixed checks. A qualifying record might enter a reminder review queue. A disputed record must take a different route. An automation is only as dependable as its inputs, rules, connections, and monitoring. A missing dispute flag is not proof that there is no dispute. If required information is unavailable, the routine path stops.

With an agent, a system might examine approved records, choose a permitted next step, and prepare a recommendation. But the task does not gain value merely because the system can take several actions. For this fixed reminder, the extra autonomy may add supervision without solving a real need. Payment, refund, and balance-changing permissions would create consequences beyond drafting. We do not grant those permissions in this exercise.

Now a customer says, I already paid, and the record still shows an unpaid balance. That contradiction changes the route. Do not send another ordinary reminder. Keep the conflicting information visible and refer the case to the accounts coordinator. The system may recommend investigation. The authorized person decides what the evidence means and approves any adjustment. This is the difference between supporting work and taking authority over it.

chapters.title: Define permissions, checkpoints and a stop route
chapters.transcript:
Return to one narrow part of your own project. Write the input and the reviewed result before describing a tool. If your project helps prepare estimate replies, the input could be an authorized request and the approved service record. The result could be a reviewed draft identifying missing details. It does not need to include booking an appointment or promising delivery. Those are different actions with different owners.

Separate four roles. Support prepares or organizes information. A recommendation suggests a next step and gives a reason. A decision selects a course of action. Approval gives permission for that action within the person's actual authority. These roles can occur close together, but they are not interchangeable. An AI suggestion saying approved cannot supply a person's approval.

Next, name allowed actions. Be specific enough that another person can tell whether the boundary was crossed. Read the supplied fictional notes. Draft a reply. Highlight a missing field. Prepare a recommendation for review. These are clearer than help with customer service. Then name prohibited actions: send to a real customer, edit an account balance, issue a refund, book an appointment, or retrieve records outside the approved scope. Include the prohibitions relevant to your project rather than copying a long generic list.

A written instruction is part of the boundary, but it is not the whole boundary. Where a system has connected tools, its actual access and settings must support the limits. If you have not checked those capabilities, record them as unverified. A product description promising human control is not evidence that your particular configuration enforces it.

Define a human checkpoint before any consequential action. Name the role, what that person checks, and what evidence allows the work to continue. A monitoring plan also needs an owner and a review rhythm. For a proposed trial, the owner might inspect every draft and record incorrect amounts or missing details. Do not describe monitoring as someone keeping an eye on things.

Finally, describe the stop and fallback route. If data is missing, contradictory, outside scope, or a required tool fails, stop the affected path. Preserve the unresolved input and give it to the named owner. State how that person can continue manually. For our invoice case, an unclear payment status goes to the accounts coordinator; no reminder or adjustment proceeds until the conflict is resolved. Keep this as a proposed design. Today's practice does not authorize deployment.

chapters.title: Verify the feature and save a defensible choice
chapters.transcript:
You now have enough detail to ask your own AI assistant for a comparison. Supply your sanitized workflow map, your intended result, and your human approval points. Ask it to compare no AI, assistant, rule-based automation, and agent support. Ask about permissions, monitoring, missing information, fallback, and uncertainty. Tell it not to propose live deployment. You remain responsible for judging the comparison.

Watch for a recommendation that skips the no-AI option or assumes that more autonomy means a better outcome. Ask which exact step requires flexibility beyond fixed rules. If the assistant cannot give a useful answer, a simpler pattern may be sufficient. If it claims a particular product can enforce an approval or access boundary, mark that as a technical claim needing evidence.

Check the current official documentation of the platform you are considering. Record the exact feature, the documentation title and address, the actual date you checked it, and what the documentation supports. Also record what remains uncertain about your account, plan, connectors, or configuration. A general help page does not prove a feature is enabled for your situation. Do not connect live accounts just to complete this lesson.

For example, Microsoft's documentation explains how Power Automate triggers start flows, how conditions select paths, and how approval flows can request a person's response. That supports a general comparison of fixed rules and approval steps. It does not prove that your proposed invoice system is configured, tested, or permitted. Likewise, an explanation of agents is useful vocabulary, not proof of a specific product's payment authority. Product names are not permissions.

If you have not chosen a platform, say so. Record that platform capabilities remain unverified and must be checked before adoption. You can still make a useful conceptual choice. For a narrow draft-and-review task, you might choose an assistant because it supports varied wording while keeping decisions and approval with a person. For a stable repetitive task, ordinary automation might be sufficient. Explain why the other three patterns are less suitable for that step.

Update your solution concept with the chosen pattern, inputs, expected result, allowed actions, human checkpoints, monitoring, stop conditions, and manual fallback. Save the four-way comparison and documentation status in your continuing Project Record. Complete the applied check by showing one action the AI may recommend but may not approve. Carry this bounded concept into Lesson Two point Five, where you will build a working sample within an authorized scope.
